query: Consider the following context: How to rationally design composition of alloys with desired properties has always been an open and challenging question, especially for high-entropy alloy (HEA) which has huge selections of composition due to the feature of multi-principal elements. Although great efforts have been made in the past decades, such as approaches based on thermo-kinetic analysis and simulations, strategies to quick determine the optimal HEA composition remain lacking. In that context, which method can be used for design intrinsically strong, ductile, and low-weight refractory HEA (RHEA) compositions, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a machine learning‐based predictive model integrated with thermodynamic analysis enables rapid identification of refractory high‐entropy alloy compositions that exhibit simultaneously enhanced strength, ductility, and reduced weight compared to alloys designed through conventional screening methods.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline refractory HEA compositions (e.g., traditional BCC refractory alloys designed via standard CALPHAD methods or limited experimental trial-and-error) with typical strength-ductility trade-offs and higher densities.
generation.intervention: Application of a data‐driven machine learning approach that integrates predictive modeling with thermodynamic analysis to rapidly screen the vast multi‐principal element composition space for candidate RHEAs.
generation.conditions: Screening and subsequent synthesis carried out under conditions relevant for both room-temperature and elevated-temperature performance; the prediction model is trained on a large, representative dataset for refractory alloy systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Optimized microstructural features such as coherent precipitate distributions within a predominantly BCC solid solution that reduce stress concentrations and allow improved dislocation mobility.
generation.mechanism: The model identifies compositional regimes that promote a favorable balance between lattice distortion (for strengthening) and workable dislocation dynamics (for ductility), while also targeting lower density through element selection, thereby overcoming the conventional strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: The computationally predicted HEA compositions will display statistically significant improvements in both mechanical performance (higher strength and improved ductility) and reduced weight relative to baseline designs.
generation.baseline: Traditional alloy design strategies (such as CALPHAD-based approaches or manual screening) which require extensive computational and experimental resources and often do not simultaneously optimize for strength, ductility, and weight.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected in refractory HEA systems with similar principal elements (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W, etc.) and when the training dataset adequately reflects the multi-element effects; deviations may occur if unforeseen minor phase formations or processing issues arise.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements remain uncertain due to limited experimental validation in the target compositional space, and external factors such as unmodeled phase transformations might affect the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Use the ML-based predictive model to rapidly screen and select several candidate RHEA compositions predicted to combine high strength, ductility, and low weight. Synthesize these predicted optimal compositions alongside baseline alloys designed via conventional methods. Perform comparative mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures) and density measurements, and conduct microstructural characterization to verify the predicted phase distributions.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile strength and ductility (% elongation)
Elevated-temperature mechanical properties (strength retention and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the candidate HEAs do not exhibit statistically significant (e.g., >10-20% improvement) simultaneous improvements in strength, ductility, and reduced weight compared to the baseline alloys, then the hypothesis that the ML-integrated approach optimizes all three properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. Here, we propose a highly efficient DFT-based method aided by a specially designed machine learning potential. As the machine learning potential can closely reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution, even for multi-component alloys, the costly thermodynamic integration can be fully substituted with more efficient free energy perturbation calculations. The method achieves overall savings of computational resources by 80% compared to current alternatives. We apply the method to the high-entropy alloy TaVCrW and calculate its melting properties

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.
